newsitem.title: FRANCE: New cast of players in Paris haute couture shows.
newsitem.headline: New cast of players in Paris haute couture shows.

text.p: The curtain goes up on whole new cast of players this weekend when the spring-summer haute couture shows open in Paris.
The first big splash comes on Sunday when London's subversive Alexander McQueen unveils his first collection for the house of Givenchy, replacing fellow Briton John Galliano.
Galliano, after just a year at the aristocratic Givenchy label, has been bumped over to Christian Dior, where he presents his first collection on Monday.

A Scot who hails from London's East End, McQueen, 27, launched his own label in 1992 in London, where his skillful cutting and penchant for blood-splattered garments and models who look as if they've just been raped have placed him on fashion's sharpest edge.

In an interview for the weekly Paris Match, the pudgy, beer-drinking rebel, one of the rare designers to talk openly to the press about his homosexuality, said his models' battered appearance was not the result of misogyny but rather his way of depicting England's "pillage and rape" of Scotland.

This is not a surprising statement from a man known for having written an insult -- and signing it -- inside a jacket he crafted for Prince Charles during his apprenticeship in the respected men's tailoring establshments of London's Savile Row.
The wording of the insult has never been disclosed.

The appointment of two of European fashion's most innovative, high-profile designers to dust off the decades-old labels is part of a clear-cut strategy by Bernard Arnault, chairman of luxury giant LVMH Moet Hennessy Louis Vuitton which owns Dior and Givenchy along with Christian lacroix, Celine and Kenzo.
Arnault recently named New York designer Marc Jacobs to launch a ready-to-wear collection for Louis Vuitton which will debut in October.
His choice of Britons for the quintessentially French houses of Dior and Givenchy has irritated many in the aristocratic world of Parisian couture.
The fact that both Galliano, the son of a plumber, and McQueen, the son of a taxi-driver, come from working-class backgrounds undoubtedly adds to the general indignation.
Adding insult to injury, McQueen doesn't even speak French.

This season also heralds the arrival of Jean-Paul Gaultier and Thierry Mugler on the couture circuit, where they'll bring the experience and financial weight of their successful ready-to-wear firms to the prestigious but loss-making art of custom-made, one-of-a-kind tailoring.
"The world of haute couture won't change its own rules. It will only happen under pressure from outside and the arrival of new designers," said Robert Bensoussan, chairman of Christian Lacroix.
The injection of young blood comes, logically, at a time when the hallowed old names of couture are gradually bowing out.

Philippe Venet and Madame Carven have been absent for several seasons, the financially ailing house of Lanvin abandoned haute couture in 1992 and Pierre Cardin has become an erratic presence on the couture catwalks.

Executives of the house of Jean-Louis Scherrer, whose label is designed by Bernard Perris, incensed by the arrival of the more plebeian ready-to-wear stylists, has also pulled off the catwalk in favour of a quiet presentation to clients and selected press members at its own salon.
